Exact uniform sampling can operate on each user’s unseen-item complement. Practical design: sort and deduplicate training-history IDs; with zero-based catalog IDs h[j], precompute a[j]=h[j]−j. Sample distinct ranks r from [0, N−|h|), then map to catalog IDs using r + searchsorted(a, r, right=True). This bijection preserves uniformity and avoids dense-user rejection; exclude padding separately. This is a derived implementation recommendation using [PyTorch searchsorted](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.searchsorted.html). For distinct ranks, randperm(M)[:K] is straightforward but allocates O(M); Floyd’s sampling algorithm is an alternative with O(K) storage. Handle K>M explicitly.

A simpler reference implementation uses equal weights on unseen items and zero weights on history, then torch.multinomial(..., replacement=False, generator=g). It supports distinct samples but requires catalog-sized weights; batching users creates O(BN) storage. Require K≤the number of unseen items. Rejection sampling remains uniform when duplicates and history items are rejected, but becomes expensive as the eligible pool shrinks. [PyTorch multinomial documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.multinomial.html).

Use explicit seeded generators, deterministic worker seeds and stable sample ordering; save generator states for resumable runs. PyTorch does not guarantee reproducibility across versions or platforms. For training, gather valid sequence positions before candidate embedding lookup, avoiding a B×L×K×D allocation for padding. Chunk valid positions and backpropagate each chunk with loss normalized by the total valid-position count; merely accumulating chunk losses retains their computation graphs. Sharing negatives across positions reduces embedding storage but changes sampling dependence. These are implementation recommendations; [PyTorch reproducibility guidance](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/randomness.html) covers RNG controls.
